findings.explanation: `res.render(view, fn)` is normalized by treating a function-valued second argument as the callback; otherwise falsey options, including `null`, become `{}`. If both the second and third arguments are functions, the second wins. The selected options object is mutated: `_locals` is unconditionally replaced with this response's `res.locals`, which the application handler normally initializes to an empty null-prototype object. Rendering is delegated to `req.app.render`. A truthy explicit callback suppresses all automatic response/error handling. Without one, the generated callback passes errors to `req.next` and successful output to `res.send`; this function itself does not explicitly set status or content type. There is no callback-type guard, so a truthy non-function can fail when delivery is attempted.

The spread order establishes precedence: `app.locals` is lowest, response locals supplied as `_locals` are next, and direct render options are highest. Thus an option passed to `res.render` overrides the same response or application local. `app.render` also treats omitted/null options as `{}`; application locals initially include `settings`. A final `cache` of `null` or `undefined` is replaced by the `view cache` setting, so `cache: null` is not an explicit disable—`false` is. The setting is enabled by default only in production, although applications may configure it. With caching enabled, the View cache is read by the exact requested `name`. A miss constructs and successfully resolves a View, inserts it at lines 567–570, and only then calls `tryRender`; consequently render failures leave that View cached. Missing views are not inserted. With caching disabled, an existing cached View is ignored but not removed. This View-object cache is distinct from the extension-keyed engine registry: a cached View retains its resolved path and engine reference, while the registry is reused even when View caching is off.

The built-in constructor first uses `path.extname(name)`. A filename extension selects that extension's engine and ignores the default engine. Without an extension, a configured default engine is required, normalized to have a leading dot, and appended to the lookup filename. Express does not configure a default `view engine`, so an extensionless name throws unless the application sets one. A truthy extension entry in `opts.engines` is reused. The normal `app.engine` API normalizes its extension and rejects non-function callbacks; if no entry exists, the constructor requires the extension-named module, reads `.__express`, verifies it is a function, and stores it in the shared registry before filesystem lookup. Module-loading errors and an absent/non-function `__express` therefore throw synchronously, potentially before a missing file can become a missing-view callback. Successfully loaded engines remain registered even if lookup later fails. Direct registry mutation can bypass `app.engine`'s function guard. These rules are proven only for the default built-in View; `app.set('view', CustomView)` replaces this constructor and its selection/loading behavior.

Built-in `lookup` converts the configured `views` value to an ordered root list and examines roots sequentially until one resolves. The default root is `path.resolve('views')`, but it is configurable and may be an array. Within each root, the resolver first checks the direct filename, then `<filename-without-extension>/index<extension>`. Therefore an index file in an earlier root wins over a direct file in a later root. Each candidate is accepted only when `fs.statSync` succeeds and `isFile()` is true; directories and other non-files fall through. `tryStat` catches every stat exception, not merely “not found,” and treats it as an unavailable candidate. If both candidates fail, resolution continues with the next root. Exhausting all roots leaves `path` as `undefined`, which is the unsuccessful lookup result later converted by `app.render` into a missing-view error.

A constructor that returns normally but has no truthy `view.path` produces an `Error` carrying `err.view` and calls `done(err)` immediately; because built-in lookup is synchronous, this missing-view delivery is synchronous and the View is not cached. In contrast, `new View(...)` is outside `tryRender`, so constructor failures—including no default engine, module-load/`__express` failures, invalid custom constructor behavior, or lookup exceptions not swallowed by `tryStat`—escape synchronously without callback delivery. Once construction succeeds, `tryRender` (lines 625–630) wraps only the call to `view.render`: a synchronous throw from a custom View or from a synchronously executing engine is caught and passed to the callback. Throws occurring in a later asynchronous engine callback, or in a next-tick callback, are outside that boundary. With the default callback installed by `res.render`, delivered errors go to `req.next`; constructor throws bypass that handler. An explicit response callback receives delivered errors itself and suppresses automatic `next`/`send` behavior.

The built-in View invokes the configured engine with `(path, options, onRender)`; because it is called as `this.engine(...)`, the engine's invocation receiver is the View. If the engine invokes `onRender` before returning, all callback arguments and the callback-provided `this` are copied and delivered on `process.nextTick`. If it invokes later, `sync` is already false and the outer callback is invoked immediately in that later call's stack, using the same arguments and context. Promise returns are ignored; completion requires the callback. Because engines and even the View class are configurable, the source cannot prove which timing or call count an actual engine uses, and a custom View need not provide this normalization. There is no `once` guard: every engine callback invocation is forwarded. Moreover, an engine can call back synchronously and then throw; the callback is already scheduled while `tryRender` catches the throw and calls the outer callback with the error, producing another later delivery. The implementation therefore does not guarantee at-most-once callback delivery.
